Directions: Read the passage below, then answer each question that follows.
Context: This excerpt was posted on the Defenders of Wildlife website in `2011`.
Title: [Excerpt from] “Sprawl Threatens Wildlife and Habitat”
Content: More than `text(one-third)` of the known species in the United States are considered in danger of extinction (Stein et al. `2000`). The main threat to these species, and biodiversity in general, is habitat loss and fragmentation. While habitat can be consumed and altered in numerous ways, poorly planned development and unmanaged growth, or sprawl, is `text(one)` of the major contributors. In a recent California study, sprawl was found to be the leading cause of species imperilment (National Wildlife Federation `2001`).

Sprawl, especially through the building of impervious* surfaces and roads, destroys and fragments habitat and disrupts ecological processes. Invasive species thrive and pollution increases in these disturbed environments, causing numerous additional problems for species and their habitat.

Sprawl has been devouring land and habitat at an alarming pace. The rate of sprawl in the United States almost `text(quadrupled)` between `1954` and `1997` and `text(doubled)` between `1992` and `1997`. About `text(3 million acres)` (roughly the size of Connecticut) of mainly forestland, pastureland, rangeland, and cropland are converted to urbanized landscapes `text(annually)` (U.S. Department of Agriculture `1997`).

The rate of development in the United States `text(doubled)` in the last `text(decade)` with some `text(3 million acres)` of farmland, forestland, and wildlife habitat now converted `text(annually)` — an area the size of Connecticut (Environmental Protection Agency `2001`). Currently, the rate of land consumption outpaces population growth. For example, Chicago suburbs experienced a `46%` increase in land consumption during the last `text(decade)` while only increasing population by `text(4 percent)` (Benfield et al. `1999`). And `text(once)` converted, these urbanized landscapes no longer provide the same options for wildlife, thus displacing or eliminating many species, especially those that depend upon large blocks of forest, shrubland, or grassland.

Studies show that habitat loss is the leading threat to endangered and extremely rare species. In a study of `text(1,207)` rare U.S. species that suffer from habitat loss, `text(35 percent)` are threatened by commercial development and `38%` by agricultural development (Wilcove et al. `2000`). Since most agricultural development occurred `text(years)` ago commercial development is now the most immediate threat.

`ultext(Lowland habitat)`. In the United States, the most biologically diverse areas occur in low-elevation bottomlands, the same places where most major cities are located. Unfortunately, biodiversity has been much better protected at the high elevations than the lower elevations (Scott et al. `2001`). Habitat loss in the lowlands has severed connections between populations, creating isolated habitat islands for species that would otherwise move through valleys (Shafer `1990`, Saunders et al. `1991`). In addition, road mortality and human-species conflicts occur when developed areas block the paths of animals looking to disperse, migrate, and locate suitable habitat.

`ultext(Wetlands)`. Many species depend upon wetland habitat to support some stage in their life cycle. At the same time, human demand to develop these areas is high. More than `text(50 percent)` of the wetlands in the U.S. have been drained and filled (Environmental Protection Agency `2001`).

`ultext(Agricultural lands)`. Farms, if managed properly, can provide wildlife habitat for some species, but many populations of species historically associated with native prairie or forests that are now converted to agriculture have declined dramatically. In fact, grassland birds are considered the most threatened group of birds in the United States because of habitat loss (U.S. Geological Survey `1998`).

At the beginning of the `text(twentieth century)` the most significant form of habitat loss was logging and farmland conversion. Although more of the U.S. landscape has been converted to agriculture than to development, today habitat lost to development is the more pressing problem. Currently, not much new farmland is being created.
